catalog_quote: Yet another attested form of lexical gender manifestation in Ubang is tonal alternation. In certain words, tonal melody polarises across male and female speech. Tonal polarisation is used here in the sense that tones in specific syllables of cognate words consistently differ in female and male versions. This gender-based tonal opposition is usually between low and high tones, such that where the male use high tone, the females substitute with a low tone and vice versa (Table 7). Tonal polarisation is replete after the first syllable of words and has not been found in monosyllabic words. It should be noticed in Table 7 that there is a versa verse effect in Ubang tonal polarisation, such that no specific tone may be ascribed to a gender. new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for word stress is given anywhere. Ubang is presented as a lexical tone language with high and low tones on every syllable (all cited forms are tone-marked, e.g. 'bone' male Ìkébé vs female Ìkébè, 'boil' male Íntʃùɛ̀ vs female Íntʃúɛ́); male and female cognate words can differ by tone alone, and this polarisation occurs on non-initial syllables. Stress/accent is never mentioned.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. On tone: polarisation is not found in monosyllables and no gender is consistently assigned H or L (an α/-α pattern); the author leaves open how these tones behave 'in phrase with other words'.
new_statements.domain_note: Words in isolation (elicited wordlist items); the author explicitly defers phrase-level tonal interaction. Data from all three Ubang villages (Ikiro/Okiro, Ofambe, Okweriseng), male and female varieties. The source is a sociolinguistic (diglossia) article by a field linguist, not a phonological description; Idialu 2025 (p. 45) independently states tones 'serve both lexical and grammatical functions', but that paper's sourcing is unreliable.
new_statements.identity_note: Ubang proper (uban1243, ISO uba), spoken in the three villages Ikiro/Okiro, Ofambe and Okweriseng, Obudu LGA, Cross River State; both the male and the female gender varieties are covered by Lewis 2024 and Blench 2001. No dialect issue; the closest relatives Ukpe, Alege and Bete are separate Bendi languages.

sources.note: Nothing on stress. Section 'Gender-driven vowel and tonal alternations' (pp. 6-7) treats Ubang as having lexical H/L tone: cognate male/female words differ by tone polarisation (Table 7, e.g. 'boil' male Íntʃùɛ̀ vs female Íntʃúɛ́), 'replete after the first syllable of words and has not been found in monosyllabic words'; all data tone-marked. The only 'stress' hit is the idiom 'it should be stressed that'.

Paper, 32nd Annual Conference on African Linguistics, Benue-Congo Workshop, Berkeley, 26-27 March 2001, 26 pp. (Comparative on rogerblench.info; includes Ubang male and female wordlist columns.)
sources.note: The wordlist (52 Ubang rows read via the Wiktionary copy) is tone-marked (e.g. m. rì-bɛ̂ 'tongue', f. ɔ̀-ɲìɲǐɛ 'woman'), consistent with a tone language; whether the PDF's prose says anything about tone or stress could not be checked (rogerblench.info could not be reached by automated download/sgcaptcha; web.archive.org could not be reached by automated download; arquivo.pt has no capture).

sources.citation: Idialu, Princess Omovrigho. 2025. Diglossia gender-based Bendi language: the Ubang community where both sexes communicate in different languages. International Journal of Arts, Languages, Linguistics and Literary Studies (JOLLS) 14(3): 42-54. Wesley University, Ondo. Open access (AJOL, CC BY-NC-ND).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on stress. p. 45: 'Ubang's phonological system is characterised by a rich inventory of consonants and vowels, including pervasive nasalisation and tonal distinctions. Tones serve both lexical and grammatical functions, distinguishing meaning at both the word and sentence levels (Iwara, 2017).' Section 3.5 (p. 50) gives tone-marked male/female pairs. Caution: the cited 'Iwara 2017' and several other references could not be verified and at least one (Effiom, Eyo & Esemu 2020, JWAL 47(1)) is absent from that issue's table of contents; treat this paper as unreliable on sourcing.
